places.title: Old Man of Storr
places.summary: Skye's best-known landmark: a 50 m pinnacle of rock below the Trotternish ridge, reached by a steep walk of about two hours there and back.
places.content:
The Old Man of Storr is the tallest of a group of rock pinnacles standing below the cliffs of the Storr, on the east side of the Trotternish peninsula. On a clear day it can be seen from far along the coast road, and from the sea beyond.

It is the work of an ancient landslip. The Trotternish ridge is an escarpment some 30 km (19 miles) long, where a heavy cap of volcanic rock sits on weaker sediments from the Jurassic period. Long ago the edge gave way and slid towards the sea, leaving the pinnacles behind. The ground is still not entirely at rest: in the summer of 2004 large rocks fell from the cliff and came to a stop at the foot of the Old Man.

In Gaelic it is Bodach an Stòir. One local story says the pinnacle is the thumb of a giant who lies buried in the hillside; another, that the cliff shows the face of an old man.

The walk starts at the car park beside the A855. The path is well made but steep and exposed to the weather, and it climbs steadily all the way. Most people go as far as the foot of the pinnacle and the viewpoint just above it, which looks back over the Old Man to the Sound of Raasay and the mainland. Beyond that point the ground is rougher and calls for a map, a compass and hill experience.
places.directions: 11 km (7 miles) north of Portree on the A855 towards Staffin, about 15 minutes by car. The car park is on the left; in summer it fills by mid-morning.
places.best_time: Before 9:00, ahead of the tour coaches, or late in the afternoon. Summer has the long light and the crowds.
tips: Wear boots or shoes with a good grip and carry a waterproof, even on a fine morning.
The main car park has a height barrier: motorhomes and tall vans use the marked bays on the road.
If the car park is full, come back later. Parking on the verges is not allowed.
The toilets by the car park are free. A kiosk across the road sells drinks and snacks in summer.
Phone signal comes and goes on the hill, so do not rely on it to find your way.

faq.question: Why is it called the Old Man of Storr?
faq.answer: The name is a translation of the Gaelic Bodach an Stòir. Local tradition explains it in two ways: the pinnacle is the thumb of a giant buried in the hillside, or the cliff behind it shows the face of an old man.

faq.question: How was the Old Man of Storr formed?
faq.answer: By a huge landslip. The Trotternish ridge is made of heavy volcanic rock lying on softer Jurassic sediments. The edge of the ridge collapsed and slid seawards, and the pinnacles are what was left standing. Rockfalls still happen: a large one came down in 2004.

faq.question: How much is parking at the Old Man of Storr?
faq.answer: £6 for up to six hours and £8 for up to twelve, the same for every vehicle. You can pay at the machines with cash or card, or with the RingGo app. Spaces cannot be booked in advance, and the main car park holds about 140 cars.

faq.question: Can you get to the Old Man of Storr by bus?
faq.answer: Yes. Stagecoach bus 57A leaves Somerled Square in Portree for Flodigarry and stops at the Old Man of Storr after about 15 minutes; the 57C brings you back. There is no 57A on Sundays, and timetables change, so check them before you set out.

faq.question: Are there toilets at the Old Man of Storr?
faq.answer: Yes, by the car park. They are free and include baby changing; the accessible toilet opens with a radar key. Beside them there is a free waste point for motorhomes.

faq.question: Can you park a motorhome or stay overnight at the Storr?
faq.answer: Motorhomes cannot enter the main car park because of the height barrier, but there are bays for them and other large vehicles on the road. Nobody may stay overnight: use one of the campsites nearby.

faq.question: What should you wear for the walk?
faq.answer: Footwear that supports the ankle and grips on wet rock, and layers with a waterproof on top. The path is steep and open to the wind, and the weather can turn within minutes. Take water, and sunscreen in summer.

faq.question: Is there an electric car charger?
faq.answer: Yes, the car park has both fast and standard chargers. In summer they are often in use, so have a second option in mind.

places.title: Quiraing
places.summary: The largest landslip in Britain, still moving: a viewpoint by the road and a 2-hour loop walk among pinnacles, with the Needle, the Table and the Prison.
places.content: The Quiraing is the northern end of the Trotternish landslip. The road from Staffin to Uig climbs to a car park at the top of the pass; from there the view alone is worth the stop, and a path contours below the cliffs to the Prison, the Needle and the Table.
places.directions: Single-track road between Staffin and Uig. Car park at the top of the pass, pay-and-display.
places.best_time: Morning light; often windy at the top.
tips: The full loop has exposed sections; the first 20 minutes give most of the views.
Car park is small; arrive early in July–August.

places.title: Kilt Rock and Mealt Falls
places.summary: A 55 m sea cliff of basalt columns that looks like a pleated kilt, with a waterfall dropping straight into the sea. A 10-minute roadside stop.
places.content: A viewing platform right by the A855 looks across to Kilt Rock and the Mealt waterfall. On windy days the wind through the railings makes an eerie hum. Dinosaur footprints can be found on the shore at nearby An Corran, Staffin, at low tide.
places.directions: On the A855 between Portree and Staffin; signposted lay-by with car park.
places.best_time: Any time; dramatic in wind and rain.
tips: Combine with the dinosaur footprints at An Corran beach at low tide.

places.title: Fairy Glen
places.summary: A miniature landscape of grassy cone hills, a tiny loch and a rock tower called Castle Ewen, near Uig. An easy 45-minute wander.
places.content: The Fairy Glen is a small landslip area that produced dozens of rounded hillocks. Paths wind between them; Castle Ewen, the rocky outcrop, can be scrambled for the view. Please don't build stone spirals: the community removes them to protect the turf.
places.directions: Single-track road from Uig signposted Balnaknock/Sheader. Small car park; do not park on the verge.
places.best_time: Late afternoon light; avoid midday in summer.
tips: Very narrow access road: not for motorhomes.
Boggy after rain.

places.title: Fairy Pools
places.summary: Crystal-clear pools and small waterfalls on the River Brittle below the Black Cuillin. An easy 40-minute walk each way from the car park.
places.content: A well-made path follows the river up towards the Cuillin, passing a series of pools and falls. The water is cold even in August; wild swimming is popular but the rocks are slippery. The classic view is the first big pool with the mountains behind.
places.directions: From Carbost take the Glenbrittle road; large pay car park on the left after about 6 km.
places.best_time: After rain for the falls; early morning to avoid crowds.
tips: Stepping stones to cross the river can be impassable after heavy rain.
Midges in calm weather May–September.

places.title: Talisker Distillery
places.summary: Skye's oldest working distillery, on the shore of Loch Harport at Carbost. Tours and tastings most days; book ahead in summer.
places.content: Founded in 1830, Talisker makes a peaty, peppery single malt with a maritime edge. The visitor centre offers tours of about an hour ending in a tasting, plus a shop and bar. Drivers can take their drams away in a sample bottle.
places.directions: In Carbost village on the B8009. Car park at the distillery.
places.best_time: Book the tour in advance from May to September.
tips: The Oyster Shed up the hill is a local favourite for seafood.
Under-18s can join tours but not taste.

places.title: Dunvegan Castle and Gardens
places.summary: Seat of Clan MacLeod for 800 years, with the Fairy Flag, formal gardens and seal-watching boat trips from the castle jetty. Allow 2 hours.
places.content: Dunvegan is said to be the oldest continuously inhabited castle in Scotland. Inside are clan relics including the Fairy Flag and Rory Mor's drinking horn; outside, walled and water gardens drop to the loch. Short boat trips go out to the seal colony.
places.directions: 1 km north of Dunvegan village on the A850. Free car park at the entrance.
tips: Seal trips are weather dependent; buy tickets at the castle.
Dogs allowed in the gardens on a lead, not in the castle.

places.title: Neist Point
places.summary: Skye's westernmost point: a lighthouse on a headland of sea cliffs, reached by a steep concrete path. The island's best sunset.
places.content: A 20-minute walk (steep steps down, then flat) leads to the 1909 lighthouse. The famous photo is taken from the cliff top to the right of the car park, looking back at the headland. Minke whales, dolphins and basking sharks are seen offshore in summer.
places.directions: From Glendale follow the single-track road to its end; car park at the top of the cliffs.
places.best_time: Sunset; stay for the colours after the sun goes down.
tips: The access road is very narrow with few passing places; allow time.
Very exposed: hold on to hats and children.

places.title: Portree
places.summary: Skye's capital and the practical base: the painted harbour, most of the island's restaurants and shops, and the departure point for wildlife boat trips.
places.content:
Portree is the capital of Skye and its only real town. It sits around a sheltered bay on the east coast, roughly in the middle of the island, which is why most visitors use it as their base: the roads to Trotternish, Dunvegan and the south all meet here, and so do the island's buses.

The picture everyone knows is Quay Street, the row of painted houses along the harbour, now shops, guesthouses and restaurants. Bank Street, one level up, is the main street. Fishing boats still work from the pier, and wildlife trips leave from it in season.

The name is usually explained as the King's Port, after a visit by James V of Scotland, who sailed to Skye in 1540 with a fleet to settle the quarrels of the MacLeods and the MacDonalds. Two centuries later the town saw another royal visitor: in 1746 Charles Edward Stuart, on the run after Culloden, said goodbye to Flora MacDonald at the inn that stood where the Royal Hotel is today.

Ships carrying emigrants to North America left from this harbour in the 18th century, when the island could no longer feed its people. In the 19th, steamers from Glasgow made Portree the commercial centre of Skye and brought its first tourists.

Two short walks start in the town. The Lump is the wooded headland above the harbour, with an old tower you can climb for the view of the bay and the Cuillin, and a natural arena where the Skye Highland Games are held in summer. The Scorrybreac circuit follows the shore from the north side of the bay round a headland and back over the hill; seals are sometimes seen from the path.
places.directions: On the A87, 55 km (34 miles) from the Skye Bridge. Car parks are signed in the centre, which is small and best seen on foot.
places.best_time: Early evening, when the day visitors have left and the light is on the harbour.
tips: In summer, book a table for dinner: the restaurants fill and there are not many of them.
Reserve accommodation months ahead for June to September. Broadford, near the bridge, is the usual alternative when Portree is full.
The supermarket and fuel here are the last before the north of the island.
Distances on Skye take longer than the map suggests: allow extra time for every drive.

faq.question: What does the name Portree mean?
faq.answer: It comes from the Gaelic Port Rìgh, usually translated as the King's Port. Tradition links it to James V of Scotland, who anchored here in 1540 on a voyage to bring the island clans to order.

faq.question: Is Portree a good base for visiting Skye?
faq.answer: Yes, and it is the one most people choose. It is in the middle of the island, it has the widest choice of places to sleep and eat, and the bus routes to Dunvegan, Uig, Staffin and Broadford all start here. The drawback is demand: in summer it is busy and rooms sell out early.

faq.question: How do you get to Portree without a car?
faq.answer: By coach. Long-distance services run to Portree from Glasgow, Edinburgh and Inverness. From Inverness the journey takes about three and a half hours, from Glasgow about six and a half, and from Edinburgh about seven and a half. You can also take the train from Inverness to Kyle of Lochalsh and continue by bus. There is no railway on Skye.

faq.question: How long is the drive to Portree?
faq.answer: About three hours from Inverness, five from Glasgow and five and a half from Edinburgh, without stops. The usual route is the A87 over the Skye Bridge.

faq.question: Where are the coloured houses of Portree?
faq.answer: On Quay Street, along the harbour. The best view of the whole row is from the road above, on the way up to Bank Street, or from the far side of the pier.

faq.question: What is there to do in Portree?
faq.answer: Walk the harbour, climb the Lump for the view over the bay, and do the Scorrybreac circuit, a short walk along the shore and back over the hill. In season, boat trips leave from the pier to look for sea eagles and seals. The Skye Highland Games are held here in summer.

faq.question: How far ahead should you book a room in Portree?
faq.answer: For the summer months, several months ahead. The island has far more visitors than beds between June and September, and Portree is the first place to fill.

places.title: Sligachan Old Bridge
places.summary: The three-arched 1810 bridge with the Black Cuillin behind: the most painted view on Skye, a 10-minute stop at the junction of the A87 and A863.
places.content: Sligachan is where the roads to Portree and to Dunvegan part. The old stone bridge over the River Sligachan frames Sgùrr nan Gillean and the Cuillin ridge. Legend says dipping your face in the river for seven seconds grants eternal beauty. The hotel has a climbing museum and a bar with hundreds of whiskies.
places.directions: At the Sligachan junction on the A87, 14 km south of Portree. Free car park by the hotel.
places.best_time: Clear mornings for the ridge; it is often in cloud.
tips: Start of the long walk into Coire Lagan and up Sgùrr nan Gillean: experienced hikers only.
Good campsite next to the hotel.

places.title: Kyleakin
places.summary: The first village on Skye, beside the bridge: a small harbour, the ruin of Castle Moil and views back to the mainland. A common overnight stop.
places.content:
Kyleakin was where the ferry from the mainland landed until the Skye Bridge opened in 1995. The bridge tolls were scrapped in 2004 and the village is now a quiet place just off the main road, with a harbour, a few places to eat and somewhere to sleep.

On the point beyond the harbour stands what is left of Castle Moil. Local legend gives it to a Norse princess, known as Saucy Mary, who is said to have stretched a chain across the narrows to charge passing ships a toll.
places.directions: Signposted off the A87 at the Skye end of the bridge. Free parking by the harbour.
places.best_time: Evening, when the light is on the castle ruin and the bridge.
tips: The path out to the castle ruin is rough and boggy, and the last part can be awkward at high tide.
Kyle of Lochalsh, across the bridge, has the nearest supermarket, fuel and railway station.

places.title: Lealt Falls
places.summary: A waterfall dropping into a deep gorge beside the Trotternish road, seen from a viewing platform a few minutes from the car park.
places.content:
The Lealt river falls in two stages into a narrow gorge on its way to the sea. A short surfaced path leads from the car park to a platform over the upper fall, with a view along the coast and across to the mainland.

A rougher path continues to the cliff edge above the shore, where the ruins of an old diatomite works can be seen below.
places.directions: Beside the A855 between the Old Man of Storr and Kilt Rock. Signed car park on the seaward side of the road.
places.best_time: After rain, when the falls are full.
tips: Keep back from the unfenced edges beyond the platform.
Easy to combine with Kilt Rock, a short drive further north.

places.title: Eilean Donan Castle
places.summary: Scotland's most photographed castle, on a small island where three sea lochs meet, reached by a stone footbridge. On the main road to Skye.
places.content:
Eilean Donan stands on a small tidal island at the point where three sea lochs meet: Loch Duich, Loch Long and Loch Alsh. A stone bridge of three arches joins it to the shore beside the main road to Skye, which is why almost everyone on the way to the island stops here.

The island takes its name from Donan, an Irish missionary who is said to have settled here in the 6th century. The first castle was built in the early 13th century, in the reign of Alexander II, to hold this coast against Norse raiders. For most of the centuries that followed it belonged to the Mackenzies of Kintail, with the MacRaes as its keepers.

Its end came in 1719. A Jacobite rising that year had Spanish backing, and a garrison of Spanish soldiers was left in the castle with the powder store. Royal Navy ships sailed up the loch, bombarded the walls, took the garrison prisoner and blew up what remained. A few weeks later the rising was defeated at the Battle of Glen Shiel, a short way up the glen.

The ruin lay open to the weather for nearly two hundred years. Lieutenant-Colonel John MacRae-Gilstrap acquired it and rebuilt it between 1912 and 1932, working from the surviving ground plan; the bridge dates from the same works. What you visit is therefore a 20th-century castle on medieval foundations, and it now belongs to a charitable trust that looks after it and keeps it open.

Inside, the rooms are furnished as a Highland home of the 17th and 18th centuries, with a banqueting hall and an exhibition on the castle's history. Some rooms are private. The castle has also had a long career on screen, as the clan home in Highlander and as an MI6 base in The World Is Not Enough.
places.directions: At Dornie on the A87, 13 km (8 miles) east of Kyle of Lochalsh and the Skye Bridge. Car park at the visitor centre, beside the road.
places.best_time: First thing or after 16:00 in summer. The outside is floodlit after dark.
tips: Tickets are sold only at the castle on the day: there is no online booking.
Last admission is one hour before closing.
Rucksacks and large bags are not allowed inside. There are free lockers by the visitor centre.
The classic photograph is taken from the shore by the car park, and it is free.
At high tide the castle is ringed by water, which makes the better picture.

faq.question: How much does it cost to visit Eilean Donan Castle?
faq.answer: In the 2026 season an adult ticket is £13. Visitors aged 60 or over pay £12, children from 5 to 15 pay £6.50 and under-fives go free. A family ticket for two adults and three children is £38. Tickets are bought at the castle on the day; they are not sold online.

faq.question: When is Eilean Donan Castle open?
faq.answer: Every day from the start of February to 22 December, apart from a few closed days in November and December. Hours are longest in summer, 9:00 to 18:00, and shortest in winter, 10:00 to 16:00. The castle is closed for the whole of January. The dates shift a little each year, so check the official site before you travel.

faq.question: Can you see Eilean Donan Castle without paying?
faq.answer: Yes. The famous view of the castle and its bridge is from the shore next to the car park, which is open to everyone. You only need a ticket to cross the bridge and go inside.

faq.question: How far is Eilean Donan Castle from the Isle of Skye?
faq.answer: About 13 km (8 miles) from Kyle of Lochalsh, where the bridge to Skye begins: ten to fifteen minutes by car.

faq.question: Is Eilean Donan a real medieval castle?
faq.answer: The site is medieval, but the building is not. The original castle, begun in the 13th century, was blown up in 1719 and stood in ruins for almost two hundred years. It was rebuilt between 1912 and 1932 on the old ground plan.

faq.question: Why were there Spanish soldiers at Eilean Donan?
faq.answer: Spain supported the Jacobite rising of 1719 and sent troops to Scotland. Some of them were left to guard the castle, which was being used as a store for gunpowder. Royal Navy ships attacked it, captured the garrison and destroyed the castle with its own powder.

faq.question: Which films were shot at Eilean Donan Castle?
faq.answer: The best known are Highlander (1986), where it is the home of the MacLeod clan, and the James Bond film The World Is Not Enough (1999), where it appears as an MI6 headquarters. It has also been used in many advertisements.

faq.question: Can you take bags into the castle?
faq.answer: Small bags only. Rucksacks and large bags have to be left in your car or in the free lockers beside the visitor centre.

places.title: Loch Ness and Urquhart Castle
places.summary: The ruin of one of Scotland's largest castles on a headland above Loch Ness, with a visitor centre and boat trips on the loch from nearby.
places.content:
Loch Ness runs for about 37 km along the Great Glen and is more than 200 m deep, which is why it holds more water than any other loch in Scotland, and why the monster story has lasted. Urquhart Castle, on a headland on the north shore, is the best place to see it from.

The castle changed hands many times in the wars with England and was blown up in 1692 so that it could not be used again. The tower that remains can be climbed. Loch cruises leave from a pier close by.
places.directions: On the A82 about 3 km east of Drumnadrochit, on the north shore of the loch. Car park at the visitor centre.

opening_hours.hours: Daily, shorter hours in winter; check the official site

places.best_time: Outside the middle of the day in summer, when the car park fills.
tips: In summer it is worth booking a time slot in advance.
The castle and the loch cruise are separate tickets.

places.title: Inverness
places.summary: The capital of the Highlands, on the River Ness: a compact centre with the riverside, the Victorian Market and plenty of places for lunch.
places.content:
Inverness is the only city in the Highlands and the natural stop between Skye and the south. The centre is small enough to see on foot in an hour: the river with its footbridges, the castle on its hill above, and the covered Victorian Market.

If you have longer, the path along the river to the Ness Islands is a quiet walk from the centre.
places.directions: Where the A9, A82 and A96 meet. Several pay car parks in the centre.
tips: The last large supermarkets and outdoor shops before the west coast are here.

places.title: Pitlochry
places.summary: A Victorian resort town in the Perthshire hills, just off the A9: one main street of shops and cafés, and a dam with a fish ladder by the river.
places.content:
Pitlochry grew up as a holiday town after the railway arrived in the 19th century and still looks the part, with stone villas and a long main street. It is the usual place to break the drive between Inverness and Edinburgh.

Ten minutes' walk from the centre, the dam on the River Tummel has a fish ladder where salmon can sometimes be seen making their way upstream.
places.directions: Signposted from the A9, about 45 km north of Perth. Pay car parks behind the main street.
tips: Salmon run the fish ladder mainly from spring to autumn; there is no guarantee of seeing one.

places.title: Glencoe
places.summary: Scotland's most famous glen: a deep valley between steep mountains, crossed by the main road, with a dark place in Highland history.
places.content:
The road from the south climbs over Rannoch Moor and then drops into Glencoe between walls of rock. The best-known view is of the Three Sisters, three great ridges on the south side, from the lay-bys beside the road.

The glen is also remembered for the massacre of February 1692, when government soldiers who had been lodging with the MacDonalds of Glencoe turned on their hosts. A visitor centre near Glencoe village tells the story.
places.directions: On the A82 between Tyndrum and Fort William. Lay-by car parks along the glen; the Three Sisters viewpoint is signed.
places.best_time: Early or late; the lay-bys are crowded in the middle of the day.
tips: The lay-bys are small and busy: do not stop on the road itself.
Weather changes fast here; the tops are often in cloud.

places.title: Glenfinnan Viaduct and Monument
places.summary: The curving railway viaduct known from the films, and the monument at the head of Loch Shiel where the 1745 Jacobite rising began.
places.content:
The viaduct carries the West Highland Line across the glen on 21 arches. It was finished in 1901 and was one of the first large structures built in concrete. A path from the car park leads in about fifteen minutes to a viewpoint above it; in season a steam train crosses twice a day.

On the loch side of the road, the Glenfinnan Monument marks the spot where Prince Charles Edward Stuart raised his standard in August 1745.
places.directions: On the A830 between Fort William and Mallaig, about 27 km west of Fort William. Pay car parks at the visitor centre.
places.best_time: Arrive well before a steam train is due: the car parks fill.
tips: Steam train times change each season; check them before planning the stop around a crossing.
The viewpoint path is uneven and muddy after rain.

places.title: Fort William
places.summary: The main town of the west Highlands, on Loch Linnhe at the foot of Ben Nevis, the highest mountain in Britain. The usual lunch stop on the way to Skye.
places.content: Fort William is a working town rather than a pretty one, but it has what a long drive needs: a pedestrian high street with places to eat, supermarkets and fuel. Ben Nevis, at 1,345 m, rises directly behind it, though the summit is hidden from the town itself.
places.directions: On the A82. Pay car parks at both ends of the high street.
tips: The last big supermarkets before Skye are here.

places.title: Loch Garry viewpoint
places.summary: A roadside viewpoint high above Loch Garry, known because from here the loch looks like a map of Scotland.
places.content: The road to Skye climbs steeply from the Great Glen, and near the top a lay-by looks down the length of Loch Garry. Seen from this angle, the shape of the loch and its wooded shores resembles the outline of Scotland.
places.directions: A signed lay-by on the A87, a few kilometres after it leaves the A82 at Invergarry.
tips: A short stop: the view is from the lay-by itself.

places.title: Commando Memorial
places.summary: A bronze of three commandos looking towards Ben Nevis, on a hill above Spean Bridge, in memory of the soldiers who trained in these mountains.
places.content:
The memorial was unveiled in 1952 to the commandos of the Second World War, who trained at nearby Achnacarry. It stands on open ground with one of the widest views in Lochaber: Ben Nevis and Aonach Mòr to the south on a clear day.

Beside it is a small garden of remembrance.
places.directions: Beside the A82 about 2 km north-west of Spean Bridge, at the junction with the B8004. Free car park.
tips: It is a place of remembrance: families still leave tributes in the garden.

places.title: Five Sisters of Kintail
places.summary: A ridge of five pointed peaks rising straight from the head of Loch Duich: the mountain view of the drive between Skye and Loch Ness.
places.content:
The Five Sisters stand in a row along the north side of Glen Shiel, three of them above 914 m. The main road runs along their foot, and they are seen at their best looking back from the shore of Loch Duich.

The traverse of the whole ridge is a long and serious mountain day for experienced hillwalkers.
places.directions: On the A87 through Glen Shiel, between Shiel Bridge and Cluanie. Lay-bys along the road and beside Loch Duich.
tips: The tops are often in cloud; the view is best in clear weather after a front has passed.

places.title: Dunkeld
places.summary: A small Perthshire town on the River Tay, with a part-ruined cathedral on the riverbank and streets of restored 18th-century houses.
places.content: Dunkeld is a short step off the A9 and a calm place to stretch your legs. The cathedral, half ruin and half parish church, stands in lawns beside the Tay, and the old houses around the square have been carefully restored. The bridge over the river dates from 1809.
places.directions: Signposted from the A9, about 24 km north of Perth. Pay car park by the river.
tips: The Hermitage, a woodland walk to a waterfall, is a couple of kilometres away on the other side of the A9.

places.title: Stirling
places.summary: The old gateway between Lowlands and Highlands, with its castle on a rock above the plain and the Wallace Monument on the hill opposite.
places.content: For centuries whoever held Stirling controlled the way north, which is why two of the decisive battles of Scottish history, Stirling Bridge in 1297 and Bannockburn in 1314, were fought within sight of the castle. The castle and the tower of the Wallace Monument are both visible from the motorway as you pass.
places.directions: Beside the M9, about 60 km north-west of Edinburgh. Pay car park on the castle esplanade.

opening_hours.hours: Castle open daily; check the official site

tips: Seeing the castle properly takes at least two hours; from the road it is a passing view.

places.title: Callander
places.summary: A small town at the edge of the Highlands, on the road north from Stirling, and a gateway to Loch Lomond and the Trossachs National Park.
places.content: Callander sits where the flat country ends and the hills begin. Its long main street has cafés, bakeries and shops, which makes it the first comfortable stop on the way north from Edinburgh or Glasgow.
places.directions: On the A84, about 25 km north-west of Stirling. Pay car parks off the main street.

places.title: Loch Lubnaig
places.summary: A narrow loch between steep wooded hills, right beside the road north of Callander: the first real Highland scenery of the journey.
places.content: The road follows the east shore of Loch Lubnaig for several kilometres, with Ben Ledi rising on the far side. Lochside car parks give a few minutes by the water.
places.directions: Beside the A84, a few kilometres north of Callander. Signed car parks on the shore.
